Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty View image in fullscreen Rampal power plant on the Pasur River. A study found high levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples in the nearby Sundarbans wetlands. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Global development Barclays faces complaint over backing for power plant near world’s largest mangrove forest Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site Supported by About this content Matthew Pearce Wed 2 Sep 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 06.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India. Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant. The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species , including the Bengal tiger. Sharif Jamil , an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals. “The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.” Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River. Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”. View image in fullscreen The Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and one of the last habitats of Bengal tigers, supports the livelihoods of millions of people. Photograph: Bengal Picture Library/Alamy Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources. The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project. Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project. The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather. The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says. Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility. “Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.” Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?” The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal. They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school. Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.” The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint. Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment. https://www.politico.eu/article/steve-wi.text: U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow and Kyiv in the coming days in an apparent attempt to restart stalled negotiations to end the Ukraine war, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram . “We discussed today that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow and then Kyiv on Sunday,” the Ukrainian president wrote. No details about the substance of the meetings have been released, but a U.S. official told CNN Friday that Witkoff and Kushner intend to press for a diplomatic solution to end the conflict. Advertisement Advertisement Russian state news agency TASS reported that Witkoff and Kushner “intend to travel to Moscow and Kyiv on September 5-6.” The men have been key U.S. mediators in the stalled Ukraine peace talks. Witkoff made several trips to Moscow for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2025 and early 2026 and met with Zelenskyy in the U.S., Germany and France. This will be their first trip to Kyiv. After Trump returned to office in early 2025, the U.S. launched an intensive push for a Russia-Ukraine peace deal focused on territorial compromises, security guarantees for Ukraine and postwar reconstruction. Washington initially put heavy pressure on Kyiv to accept the proposals, but by early 2026, the talks broke down. In recent weeks, Washington has renewed its efforts to engage with Moscow, with CIA Director John Ratcliffe visiting the Russian capital in late August. Ratcliffe used the trip to press Russia to reduce its military and economic support to Iran and urge it not to escalate conflict with America’s NATO allies. Advertisement Advertisement

(AP Photo/Sergei Grits) WARSAW – Two people died and around half a million people were left without electricity across Latvia and Lithuania after a powerful cyclone, bringing rain and strong winds, hit the region on Saturday and into Sunday morning. “This seems to be the most severe storm in Latvia since 2005 in terms of its overall impact,” Andris Viksna, from the Latvian Environment, Geology and Meteorology Center, told the AP. Recommended Videos One person died in Jelgava, central Latvia, when part of a building collapsed on Saturday, and others were injured across the country. Wind speed exceeded 67 mph on Saturday in the capital, Riga. At many stations, half of the average monthly rainfall was recorded on Saturday. More than a quarter-million people were left without electricity and mobile services were disrupted. Rail and other public transport services were affected by trees and other objects falling on infrastructure. The Riga airport said on Sunday morning that flights could be delayed or rerouted because of the severe storm overnight. One person also died in neighboring Lithuania after being hit by a falling tree. Others were injured and over 200,000 residents were without electricity on Sunday morning. Strong winds also battered Estonia, with the western and northern parts and its islands most affected. Ferry services to islands were disrupted and trains arriving from Latvia and Lithuania delayed. Northeastern Poland was affected by the storm, too, with over 100,000 people losing power. The contribution of climate change cannot be properly assessed yet, said Viksna from the Latvian Environment, Geology and Meteorology Center, but “it is plausible that human-caused climate change may have intensified the rainfall associated with the cyclone.” The situation was expected to improve on Sunday and certainly by Monday. According to the study, overall proficiency in reading, math and science has fallen significantly among 15-year-old pupils in 90 countries, with German pupils faring particularly poorly — posting their worst scores ever in the OECD's Program for International Student Assessment, which has tracked the academic performance since 2000. "We are seeing historically low levels of proficiency," said Samuel Greiff of the Technical University of Munich. Released every three years, the 2025 assessment documented a major drop in German students' reading proficiency as well as significant dips in math and science skills since 2022 . "We aren't dramatically behind," said Greiff. "But we are not living up to our own standards as an education nation. We are not among the top performers." https://euobserver.com/235195/hungarys-a.text: More than nine months ago, we launched our Hungary Votes series , providing weekly summaries of news from Hungary’s election campaign. The series continues as we report on developments following the historic election and the measures taken by the Tisza government. This week, we cover the following topics: why the election of the head of the Asset Recovery Office has caused political tensions; how Viktor Orbán’s peculiar system for siphoning off public money is collapsing; what happened to Hungary’s state budget; what Gáspár Orbán’s wish list was all about; disarray in the Fidesz orbit. New asset-recovery boss faces difficult time Anna Unger, who was elected president of the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office on Friday (28 August), may have been given the most difficult and complex task in the history of 21st- century Hungarian politics. She must build a 150-person agency from the ground up and somehow recover the money that disappeared amid the corruption of the past 16 years. Those from whom the assets are to be recovered immediately cast themselves as victims and branded the new institution a modern-day equivalent of Hungary’s communist-era State Protection Authority. But that is not the only reason Unger’s job will be difficult. Many regard her as unfit for such an important position — among them Ákos Hadházy, a former member of parliament and anti-corruption activist. Many others believe that Miklós Ligeti, legal director of Transparency International Hungary, would have been better suited to the task. As a lawyer, Ligeti primarily promised an asset-recovery process that would be legally unassailable and built around specific cases. Unger, who is not a lawyer, wanted to give the office a broader historical and political mission: to expose the operating patterns of the System of National Cooperation, or NER, and prevent the system from reproducing itself. Of the two competing visions for the office, the narrative-driven approach ultimately prevailed. Following her election, Unger sought to explain in several interviews exactly what she was planning and what her job would entail. She also stressed that she was by no means a newcomer to the field, having extensive research and organisational experience in party financing and corruption. Nevertheless, one remark she made during her hearing began to resonate particularly strongly in public debate. Unger said it was conceivable that not a single major case would result in a final court judgement during her term. Many interpreted this as a sign that she was giving up on accountability before her work had even begun. But that is not what she meant. The Slovak example shows how cumbersome the fight against corruption can become when politics weighs heavily on the justice system. Although there was a genuine breakthrough in the investigation of corruption cases after 2020 and courts delivered judgements in numerous cases, the overall picture is far from rosy six years later. The authorities failed to catch any genuinely big fish, while high-profile trials, including the Očistec trial, only began after years of delay. In the meantime, Slovak prime minister Robert Fico returned to power, and his government abolished the Special Prosecutor’s Office and disbanded the National Criminal Agency (NAKA). NAKA played a role in investigating corruption similar to the one the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office is expected to play in Hungarian public life. Read more ‘Manual for autocrats’: how Fico’s rule-of-law breaches put Slovakia in EU sanctions crosshairs The Hungarian system is no better than the Slovak one. In fact, it bears the scars of 16 years of NER rule. On closer examination, Unger’s prediction therefore no longer seems so exaggerated. A similarly sobering assessment came from her former rival Ligeti, who estimates that only around ten percent of the assets siphoned off can realistically be recovered. More than one trillion forints recovered Asset recovery is also taking place on another front. At the end of August, the liquidation of 16 public-interest asset management foundations, known by the Hungarian acronym KEKVA, was completed. As a result, public assets worth 1,284 billion forints, or nearly €3.5bn, are returning to direct state control. The KEKVA system was created by Orbán and his allies and proved to be an exceptionally effective mechanism for siphoning off public funds. State assets and government decisions concerning them were removed from direct state control and placed in the hands of foundation boards – which were, naturally, filled with Fidesz loyalists. The board of the Mathias Corvinus Collegium Foundation, which held assets with a book value of nearly 575 billion forints, was chaired by Balázs Orbán, Viktor Orbán’s political director. The Future Generations’ Land Foundation was chaired by János Lázár, one of Orbán’s most powerful allies. The Blue Planet Climate Protection Foundation was headed by former president János Áder, while the Foundation for Hungarian Culture was chaired by Szilárd Demeter, Orbán’s Transylvanian-born cultural guru. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm36.text: Image source, REUTERS/Salahuddin Image caption, Aleema Khanum, pictured in January 2025 outside Adiala jail, speaking to the media after her brother's jail sentence By Carrie Davies ,Â Pakistan correspondent Â and Â Hafsa Khalil Published 1 hour ago The sister of Pakistan's imprisoned former prime minister, Imran Khan, has been arrested ahead of next week's protests held in his support, his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party has said. Aleema Khanum was detained in the eastern city of Lahore on Sunday afternoon, PTI officials said, calling it an "illegal detention". Her son is demanding her return. The order for Khanum's arrest, which came from Lahore's deputy commissioner, alleged that she was mobilising Imran Khan's supporters "through social media and public meetings". It added that she will be detained for 30 days. Khanum is a vocal critic of her brother's detention, regularly speaking to his supporters and the media. A police official confirmed Khanum's arrest to the BBC. According to the order, she will be taken to Kot Lakhpat jail in Lahore. Earlier in the day, her family said they had had "no contact or news of her whereabouts". "We demand the government immediately disclose her whereabouts and ensure her safe return," Khanum's son Shahrez Khan wrote on X. Many have linked her arrest to the protests that have been organised across the country on 27 September, when demonstrators plan to march to the Pakistani capital, Islamabad. The arrest order said Khanum had been mobilising people to "create law and order situations" and "raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the Government." Streets in Islamabad are already lined with shipping containers, ready to safeguard the city's government buildings. Local media has reported Pakistan's interior minister as saying that the protests harm the country and that the government will do everything they can to stop them. Khan has been detained since 2023, when he was sentenced to three years in prison for not declaring money earned from selling gifts he had received while in office. He has faced charges in over 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts - all of which he has decried as politically motivated. Last year, the cricket star-turned-politician was jailed for 14 years in a land corruption case - the longest sentence he has received. While in prison, his health has being deteriorating, and last month Khan had to visit a hospital for an examination . https://www.dw.com/en/lithuanian-skies-a.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NHze Sinkevicius said that 'if Lithuanian skies are safe, then NATO's skies are largely protected as well' Image: Denis Kishinevskiy/DW Advertisement Lithuania is on NATO's eastern flank, bordering Belarus and Russia's Kaliningrad region. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, security has become one of the country's central political priorities. The 42-year-old Mindaugas Sinkevicius recently took over as prime minister and also leads Lithuania's Social Democratic Party, a moderate center-left political force. In an exclusive interview with DW, he said he is concerned by the growing popularity of populist and far-right parties across Europe , particularly in Western Europe. But he also argued that the picture is more complicated, pointing to Social Democratic governments in several European countries and signs of renewed support for the center-left elsewhere. For Lithuania, the war in Ukraine is closely connected to its own security. The country has experienced a series of incidents involving drones , instrumentalized migration and weather balloons entering its territory from Belarus. Sinkevicius said these developments have contributed to a broader sense of insecurity across Europe. "As politicians, we have to tell society the truth," he said, identifying air defense as Lithuania's most urgent security priority. "Lithuania's airspace is NATO's common airspace. Lithuanian skies are NATO skies," he said. "If Lithuanian skies are safe, then NATO's skies are largely protected as well." Drone incidents in Lithuania and beyond Sinkevicius said Lithuania is seeking greater solidarity from its allies, pointing out that the threat goes beyond its national borders. A series of incidents involving drones have affected other European countries as well. Sinkevicius stressed that NATO membership does not mean Lithuania can simply rely on its allies. Collective defense, he argued, works only when individual members are prepared to contribute. How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "Of course, there is Article 5 . Of course, there is collective defense," he said, referring to the NATO pact. "But at the same time, we need to do certain things ourselves, rather than relying solely on our partners, neighbors and alliances." For Lithuania, this means strengthening its own deterrence capabilities while continuing to work through NATO and regional partnerships. He also pointed to the Nordic-Baltic Eight, or NB8, as an important framework for cooperation between the countries of Northern Europe and the Baltic states. National security climbs national agenda Sinkevicius rejected the idea that European countries should choose between traditional military equipment and newer technologies such as drones. "Sometimes we see these issues being pitted against each other: drones versus tanks," he said. "I say we need both." But for the Lithuanian prime minister, military equipment only goes so far. "Neither drones nor tanks will protect us if society does not feel safe, if people do not feel a connection with the state," he said. Ex-Lithuanian FM: 'We are on a trajectory of escalation' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video For Sinkevicius, that connection is linked to social policy as well as defense. He argued that a state must also support people who are unemployed, ill or otherwise vulnerable. The argument reflects a broader challenge for Sinkevicius as leader of Lithuania's Social Democratic Party. Traditionally, Social Democrats have focused more on social policy, education and healthcare than on defense. Russia's war against Ukraine has changed the political environment, forcing center-left governments in Europe to place national security much higher on their agendas. Sinkevicius said the challenge is to increase defense capabilities without abandoning the principles of social democracy. 'We will continue to support Ukraine' Sinkevicius recently traveled to Kyiv and Lutsk, some 400 kilometers (250 miles) west of the capital, where he met with Ukrainian political leaders. Lithuania has committed to allocating at least 0.25% of its GDP annually to support Ukraine. According to figures cited by the Ukrainian side, Lithuania's support in recent years has amounted to around 0.3% of GDP. The prime minister acknowledges that some degree of war fatigue exists in Europe. But he said European societies should consider the scale of what Ukrainians have experienced. "I sometimes ask myself: if we Europeans feel tired, then what must Ukrainian society be feeling?" he said. Sinkevicius also pointed to the key role of Western European countries, particularly Germany, in maintaining support for Ukraine. "Support and assistance must continue," he said. "Because if the Western front, figuratively speaking, weakens and falters, then on the eastern front — where Russia is fighting Ukraine — the risk of failure increases." https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Sailors onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln wave their hats as the carrier returns home to San Diego. Photograph: Mike Blake/Reuters View image in fullscreen Sailors onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln wave their hats as the carrier returns home to San Diego. Photograph: Mike Blake/Reuters US military Thousands turn out to welcome weary USS Lincoln sailors after record-breaking deployment Military families admit ‘mixed emotions’ as aircraft carrier finally returns to San Diego after grueling stretch at sea that took severe toll USS Lincoln arrives at San Diego base – live updates Amanda Ulrich in San Diego Thu 8 Oct 2026 18.25 EDT First published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 16.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google By 4am on Thursday, the sky still pitch black, 19-year-old Pvt Grayden Monroe and his mom had already arrived to the naval base in San Diego, California , the very first military family members huddled on a set of metal bleachers overlooking the dark water. They were waiting for Monroe’s 21-year-old sister to step off the USS Abraham Lincoln, the embattled aircraft carrier that has been at sea for the better part of a year. Monroe, a soldier stationed at Fort Campbell, was wearing his army uniform for the occasion. “I hope she’s proud of me,” he said of his sister, “and I hope she knows damn well that I’m just as proud of her.” As the sun rose over Naval Air Station North Island, thousands of people flooded on to the base for the USS Lincoln’s long-awaited return. The atmosphere was like a de facto festival, with a live band, performers on stilts, therapy dogs, handmade signs, giant cutouts of sailors’ smiling faces. People cried, laughed, screamed with joy. When the Lincoln appeared in the middle distance around noon, rounding the corner past downtown, cheers erupted from around the bay. Sailors flanked the edges of the ship in uniform, waving to the crowd and making phone calls to loved ones. Below American-flag bunting, rust stains were visible on the sides of the carrier. The massive, city-like ship had finally reached land. View image in fullscreen An onlooker cheers as the Lincoln approaches the port of San Diego. Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Military families and friends had longed for this moment for months. The Lincoln first left San Diego last November, with an expected return date sometime in the spring. But as the US and Israel launched a war with Iran, the aircraft carrier was diverted to the Middle East , extending the deployment for the roughly 5,000 sailors and marines onboard for a then-unknown amount of time. The Lincoln’s deployment ended up spanning 321 days, including 264 consecutive days at sea without a port call, a record in modern naval history, the Department of Defense said . For months, sailors have reported hazardous living conditions onboard the Lincoln: shortages of food and basic supplies, a spate of suicide attempts and a general sense of deteriorating mental health and declining morale. The reports immediately set off a political firestorm, with Democratic lawmakers calling for an investigation , even as Donald Trump and the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth , sought to downplay the situation. The US navy confirmed last month that eight service members from the Lincoln and its accompanying strike group had attempted suicide since the start of the deployment. After the Lincoln’s return home was officially announced in August, it took the carrier almost two long months to get back to San Diego, making a brief port call in Thailand and then tracing a route east across the Pacific Ocean. But on the naval base on Thursday, the scene wasn’t completely euphoric. An infant in a stroller was positioned with a sign that read “I have waited 234 days to hug my daddy!” The baby’s mom, Brenda Rivas, said she was five months pregnant when her husband deployed. He missed the birth, and the first time he was able to see his daughter over a video call was six months later. View image in fullscreen Brenda Rivas with her seven-month-old daughter. Photograph: Amanda Ulrich “It’s mixed emotions,” Rivas said. “I’m more sad than excited because he did miss so much.” And an emotional reunion on the pier wasn’t in the cards for everyone, especially for the many military families that are spread across the country. Dawn, a mother who requested that only her first name be used because she feared retaliation from military officials, anxiously watched a live feed of the ship’s arrival from a small town in Texas, her eyes “glued to the TV” for hours. Her son is a service member on the Lincoln. “I couldn’t sleep. Tossed and turned,” she texted early on Thursday morning. “I’m feeling so happy for my granddaughter to see her daddy!” Imagining that the scene in San Diego would be too chaotic, Dawn is instead flying to California next week to reunite with her son and his five-year-old daughter. She’s planning to help him “get everything back in order”: make sure his house is clean, whip up some home-cooked meals. Over the past 11 months, one thing has been keeping her son sane and tethered to a reality off the ship, she said. “He said that all he could think about was his daughter,” she said. “That’s what got him through all this.” Months of dwindling rations, worsening mental health As the sailors floated around the globe for the past year, their relatives sat at home and waited, wondering what could be happening thousands of miles away on the ship. Dawn’s son sent her updates via WhatsApp whenever he got service. This past spring, he told her, the conditions were dire. “Like 3rd world …” he wrote in a message. “We couldn’t get soap or toothpaste.” He sent her pictures of mold dripping down the walls, of dwindling daily rations: sectioned cafeteria trays with only a few of the compartments full. Two hard-boiled eggs and watery soap. A scoop of grits and a few limp noodles. View image in fullscreen Crew members on the deck of the Lincoln on Thursday. Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images The extended deployment, long working hours and supply shortages seemed to be taking their toll across the ship, especially on the younger sailors, Dawn said. Nearly half of all active-duty military members are 25 years old or younger . She could imagine her son, who’s now in his 30s, being like a father figure to some who were really struggling. The reports of some sailors attempting to jump overboard were true, her son told her. “My son’s a tough kid, so he could take it,” she said during a phone interview last week. “But for those 19-year-old kids that go on a first deployment, it’s scary for them.” One of the worst parts for Dawn was the unsolicited commentary, on Facebook and Instagram and in real life, saying that even if the ship’s conditions were rough, the sailors probably just couldn’t hack it. “That’s exactly what people were saying about the people in the military: that they’re babies, and that back in 1969, or whenever they were [serving], it wasn’t like that,” she said. “I couldn’t even read the comments. I’m still upset about it.” Those sentiments even came from Trump, who told reporters this summer that the Lincoln’s deployment was “ not nearly long enough ”. That type of remark changed everything about how Dawn viewed the president. “I like President Trump. I voted for him. But I don’t really think he understands,” she said. “Let his son be out there, just for a couple days, and see how it goes. If he really would tolerate that, if his son could really take it – I’m sure he couldn’t.” In a brief press conference on the naval base Thursday, Capt Daniel Keeler, the commanding officer of the Lincoln, answered several questions from journalists about the consistent reports of poor conditions on the ship. “[Most of those issues] occurred in March and April, while we were engaged in active combat operations against a very determined foe,” he said. “Immediately once combat operations started, we were, I would say, a little bit challenged to get the normal fill of things. But I had enough food, I had all the supplies I needed to conduct combat. We never missed a mission. I also never missed a meal.” Meanwhile, Hegseth again played down those same issues on Wednesday, saying instead that “a few folks in the media” aimed to “turn” the ship’s deployment “into some sort of symbol of dysfunction, or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission.” Keeler focused most of his comments this week on the success of the mission. “For most of my sailors, this was their first time away from home, their first deployment, their first experience with combat,” he said. “I understand the anxiety that might have caused, but I can tell you this: our team of professionals on the ship led every single one of those sailors through that experience. And the great majority responded how sailors always do, with honor, courage and commitment.” Temporary rest, shifting political views Now that the Lincoln has returned home after an unexpectedly grueling and high-profile deployment, sailors are left to determine what’s next. Some of those next steps are immediate. Monroe, the 19-year-old, said his family was excited to take his sister out to dinner tonight – but then she’s back on duty tomorrow. After the trials of the past year, a more serious takeaway for Monroe is his sense of what could happen during a deployment, and just how tough that isolation could be. “When shit hits the fan, everything just kind of sucks. Especially when they’re out there on their own. It’s really just you and the guy next to you,” he said. “So getting stuck there and being able to push through something like that – I don’t think I could have done it, honestly.” His sister, he added, was “probably one of my biggest role models”. View image in fullscreen People turn out in San Diego to welcome the USS Abraham Lincoln home. Photograph: Mike Blake/Reuters For Rivas, the wife whose husband missed their daughter’s birth, she’ll have to switch from being a single parent for a year to parenting as a team again. “It’s gonna be different, teaching him how to take care of her,” she said. “But she’s good with people, so I’m sure she’ll adjust.” For Dawn, as a Texan and someone who says she still wouldn’t vote for a Democrat, she walked away from the USS Lincoln experience with a very different outlook on Trump. The majority of those in her small town and in her family are lifelong Republicans, but the controversy surrounding the Lincoln has cut jaggedly across traditional party lines. “It’s really hard for me because I just wanted [my son] to be OK. And I just, I don’t know …” she said, her voice trailing off over the phone. “I’m just not real happy with President Trump right now. At all.” As for what her son thinks about the fraught deployment, she said, it’s probably too soon to tell how this experience will shape his life and career. But it has put some things into perspective. “He just wants to live for his kid,” she said. “He wants to see his daughter grow up.” Explore more on these topics US military California San Diego Trump administration Pete Hegseth West Coast US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
